To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the levels of serum steroids, AA, and ER levels in the preoptic area, the hypothalamus, the amygdala, and the serum do not differ in B6D2 F1 male house mice, which differ in the display or copulatory behavior after the removal of the testes.
castration of B6D 2F1 male hybrid mice reduces aromatase in the preoptic area, the hypothalamus, the amygdala, and the anterior pituitary.

castration of B6D1F1 hybrid male house mice reduced aromatase activity in preoptic area and hypothalamus, which is consistent with the hypothesis that aromatase activity mediates the effects of testosterone on the display of copulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of nongonadal estradiol in the regulation of sexual behavior in castrated male mice.
identifying the neural mechanisms that control the display of male copulatory behavior.
the neurobiology of male sexual behavior.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the B6D2 male mouse is a good animal model for studying the effects of nongonadal estrogen on copulatory behavior.
continuers have a more robust response to nongonadal estradiol than noncontinuers.
the POA, AM, and HYP have the capacity for estrogen synthesis and that these brain areas contain nuclear ER that are sensitive to circulating nongonadally derived E2.

continuers and non-continuers are similar with respect to the levels of serum steroids and the levels of aromatase activity and estrogen receptors in the preoptic area, amygdala, and hypothalamus.
